stories.title_en: Using Silver to Turn the Tables and Seduce a Woman Drying Paper

paragraphs.en: Yu Chong of Zonghua was a man of ample means and lecherous by nature. He often lent silver and grain at interest in the countryside. Villagers were home only for their morning, noon, and evening meals; before and after midday they were all out plowing the fields, leaving no men at home. Chong made a point of going to collect debts just before noon. When he found a woman alone, he tried every way to seduce her, and he often got her into bed.

Someone asked him: "When you first meet a woman, you are strangers, with no feeling between you. How can you open your mouth with indecent talk? If she flies into a rage and scolds you, how will you ever enter her door again?" Chong said: "Seducing a woman depends on reading the moment and using whatever the situation offers. You may bait her with words, tempt her with profit, press her with rank, or plead—there is more than one way. The whole art is to watch her mood and hit it. If there is no opening, try telling her a dream: say that last night you dreamed you went to a place that looked just like her house, this thing here, that thing there; and you dreamed you were with her all night, then woke and found it was a dream; and today you arrive, and it is exactly as in the dream. Tell it with a smile. Watch whether her face is pleased or angry, whether she ignores you, answers, or grows suspicious—then you know how to speak. If she scolds, I say it was only a dream. If she does not refuse, I can proceed. I once went to collect a debt. The men were making paper elsewhere; two co-sisters-in-law were drying paper facing each other. The elder brother's wife was an older woman; the younger brother's wife was very young and pretty. I wanted to seduce the younger one. If she made even half a sound of refusal, it would be heard across the drying rack—how could I act? I thought of a plan. I wrapped a single lump of silver worth one qian and said quietly: 'I want to seduce your sister-in-law. I'll give you this one qian; here is another packet of five fen—please pass it to her and intercede for me.' The woman took four packets of silver, opened her own packet, saw the silver in a lump, and was somewhat pleased. She answered: 'If you like her, tell her yourself. Of course I'll help, but I shouldn't be the one to speak.' I said: 'If I like anyone, I like you. I only feared you would refuse, so I asked you to speak to your sister-in-law.' She did not answer. I embraced her, and she silently consented. We did it with only the drying rack between us; the other side never knew. If I had not done it this way, she would have thought twice. She would have feared her sister-in-law would know, and would never have silently agreed. Only by first saying I wanted the sister-in-law would she think: 'If that side can do it, I can do it quietly here too—what's the harm?' So it was done without effort."

Note: Women who do not love lust still love money, but they deeply fear being found out, so they dare not act. Only when you give them the nerve by saying no one can know will they dare to go ahead. Once they have agreed to you, their cover-up becomes even more careful. This is one of Yu Chong's tricks to seduce a woman. But worldly wickedness has many deep, hidden schemes—how can they all be told as warnings? I only pick what I have recently heard.

stories.title_en: A Monk Cuts Silk to Swindle a Tenant's Wife

paragraphs.en: Shoushan Temple held a grain tax quota of five hundred shi, divided among twelve monastic branches. The monks were all well-off, wearing silk, eating meat, drinking wine, and visiting prostitutes—worse than laypeople. After managing the temple for ten-odd years, if they had accumulated enough silver and wished to return to lay life, they would first arrange a marriage within their family, then let their hair grow out under the guise of wandering ascetics (toutuo). Once their sideburns were long enough to be bound in a hairnet, they returned home, married, and took charge of a household. Brothers succeeded brothers; sons succeeded fathers. They treated the position as hereditary property, and no outsider could intrude. Some who feared the burden of family life and did not wish to return to the lay world would instead select a simple, honest tenant in the village who had no wife, pay silver to marry one for him, and then sleep with her for a month before handing her over to the tenant. She remained at the monk's disposal whenever he visited: when the monk arrived, she was his wife; when he left, she was the tenant's. Hence the saying: "It is not the monk who seduces the tenant's wife—it is the tenant who sleeps with the monk's woman." That was the custom. If a child was born and the timing made paternity clear, the child belonged to that father; if the timing was mixed and uncertain, the monk and the tenant split the children, each taking one. When the boys reached ten or so, the monks brought them into the temple as novice attendants—in truth, their own sons. Hence the monks had a saying: "Put out the lamp to pass on the Dharma; borrow a surname to carry on the line." That is what they meant.

One monk went to the village to collect the field rent. The tenant was timid. Seeing that the wife was pretty, the monk made advances whenever he could; she always cursed him and paid him no mind. Later, in the tenth month of winter, he deliberately bought a bolt of good silk, asked this woman to lend scissors, cut off two chi, and said, "I'll give this to someone for shoe tops." He left the rest in her hands. Two days later he came again for the silk, borrowed the scissors, cut another two chi to give someone, and left the rest with her again. The woman said, "Who are you giving it to? Why not take it all?" The monk said, "This much is enough; it will last a long time." The woman said, "If I'm storing it for you, you should cut two chi for me too." The monk said, "If you want it, I'll give you the whole bolt, and these two chi as well—no need to give that other person." The woman said, "Truly?" The monk said, "I only feared you wouldn't take it; I've long meant to give it to you." Then they soon consummated their affair. The monk said, "You used to curse me; why so kind today?" The woman said, "This winter I need a set of clothes as a birthday gift for my mother, so I had no choice but to go along. After this I certainly will not." The monk said, "Those two chi will cost one more time." The woman said, "Give the two chi to someone else." The monk said, "You take much but give back little—what a cunning woman you are!"

When they had finished and left the room, the monk said, "I need rice straw to twist a rope." The woman fetched some. The monk twisted the straw slowly. She urged him to hurry up. The monk said, "What harm in being outside?" Soon the tenant returned and asked, "What do you need the rope for?" The monk replied, "I have most of a bolt of silk to sell. Your wife said she wants it to make clothes for your mother-in-law’s birthday, and offered to pay with a pig you raised—two taels and two qian for the silk. This rope is to lead the pig away." The tenant cursed his wife: "I need to raise that pig! Why trade it for useless silk? Give it back at once!" The wife picked up two chi of the silk, threw the rest back, and said, "Take it as a gift!" The monk retorted, "I was paying you a fair price; I wasn’t cheating you. What do you mean, ‘gift’?" Seeing she had kept the two chi, he knew she still loved money. The next month he bought half a bolt of blue silk and brought it along with the earlier piece. The wife cursed, "You shaven beast belong in snail hell—I won’t even look at you!" The monk said, "Precisely because you always curse me, I deliberately took it back to make you angry. Otherwise, would I be stingy? You said you needed a full set of clothes for the birthday. Last time I gave only one piece; now I’ve respectfully cut another so you can finish the job. Why curse again?" She refused. He pleaded again and again. Since they were already intimate, she could not hold out forever and accepted again. After that, they continued their affair; it could no longer be stopped.

Note: This woman was fiery by nature; only because she loved the silk did she stain herself. As the saying goes, "When desire takes hold, how can one be firm?" Households should simply forbid monks and Daoists from coming and going—that is already a good thing. Entering temples, worshipping Buddha, giving a child a monk's or Daoist's surname—these are all shameful; be sure to avoid them. Do not chase phantom merit, only to step into endless filth.

stories.title_en: A Geomancer Leaves His Wife Behind to Steal a Fine Lineage

paragraphs.en: There was a geomancer named Lu, quite skilled at reading mountains, who wanted to find a fine gravesite to bury his own father. Searching as far as Ningcheng, he found an auspicious fengshui spot behind the ancestral shrine of the retired official Yang, where it was neither easy to buy openly nor possible to bury in secret. Hearing that Official Yang had passed away and his two sons were also looking for a site to bury their father, Geomancer Lu offered them this spot and led the two young masters to inspect it. It was indeed a fine burial site—it cost them nothing to buy, and its orientation promised great fortune. They buried their father there and rewarded the geomancer with thirty taels of silver. Since Lu could not get the gravesite for himself, he resolved to steal their lineage instead. He rented a house by the garden gate of the Yang sons, used the silver to marry a beautiful woman, and lived with her for two months. Then he told his wife: "I must travel afar to practice geomancy, and I cannot say when I will return. If the household runs short of firewood and rice, I have asked the young masters to look after you. They are my benefactors; it was only because of their silver that I could marry you. While I am away, if these two young masters make advances, you may go along with them. If you win their affection, they will support you generously later on. However, their household has many servants—never have anything to do with the servants. If you cheapen yourself, the young masters will despise you, and you will end up in poverty with no one to help." He also went to ask the two young masters: "I have to travel far away, and my household is left with meager means. Please help look after my wife, and when I return I will repay everything in full."

The young masters often visited the garden, saw that the wife was beautiful, and were already stirred. Two days after the geomancer left, the elder son came to the house and seduced her. The woman, having received her husband's instructions, readily consented, and they became deeply involved. After about a month, the younger son also came and seduced her; she consented again. Half a year later, Geomancer Lu returned, saw that rice and vegetables were plentiful, and asked his wife: "Did the young masters come?" She replied: "Both came; I took them both." Lu said: "Being with such good men brings you no shame. You have food and clothes, someone to sleep with, people looking after you morning and evening; I can rest easy even when away." The wife laughed: "The provisions are even better than when you were home—just don't get jealous." The geomancer said: "It was their silver that bought you, and they supply your needs in my place—why be jealous? But if both come in turn, you might catch the pox. Set it as one month each, and you won't get sick."

When Lu went away again, the young masters came calling once more. The woman said, "If the two of you come at irregular times, I fear I may develop a bad illness. It would be better to set odd months for the elder young master and even months for the younger." The young masters agreed: "You are quite right. From now on, each month belongs to the appointed one, and he shall supply all the vegetables, rice, and provisions." Before they knew it, four years had passed, and she had borne two sons, both of the two young masters' bloodline. Geomancer Lu had their fortunes read, and every diviner predicted great wealth and rank for them in the future. He then took his wife and sons and bade farewell to the two young masters, each of whom gave him generous parting gifts. Later, the two boys grew up and both passed the imperial examinations—in truth, the Yang family's auspicious fengshui had been secretly siphoned away without their ever knowing it.

Note: Sons of rich families often lust after other men's wives. If children result, their fengshui is inevitably split away. Observe how the lineage was cheated out of its seed—later generations should take warning from this.

A rich young man went to a tenant's house to collect rent, saw the wife was beautiful, and propositioned her repeatedly. She dared not consent and secretly told her mother-in-law. The mother-in-law said, "He's a rich man's son; if you bear him a child, later we'll have something to eat." The rich man propositioned her again; she agreed, and they went into the room to undress. He asked, "You always refused before; why agree now?" She replied, "I've already told my mother-in-law." He asked, "Does she want to catch us in the act?" She said, "No. She said to lean on your rich-family seed; if there's a son, we'll have something to eat." Upon hearing this talk of sowing seed, he suddenly realized his folly, shouting, "No! No!" four times. Then he changed his tone: 'I didn't really mean to harm you; I only admired your beauty, so I was just playing. Here are three qian of silver for powder; I won't defile you.' Still stirred by lust, he hurried home and slept with his wife that night. She conceived immediately; later, a son was born who grew up to pass the jinshi examination and became a county magistrate.

On the first day of taking office, under a clear sky, he suddenly saw two golden characters "Must Not" on each of the four great pillars of the hall. He worried: "I must not take this post." He served carefully for one season, then feigned illness and resigned to care for his parents, hurrying home. His father asked in alarm. He answered: "On the day I took office, I saw four golden "Must Not" signs; fearing they were not auspicious, I resigned to return home and care for you." The father said: "You can care for your parents while still in office." After a night, the father thought it over and was overjoyed. He called his son: 'Those four golden "Must Not" are a great auspicious sign; your career will soar. When I was young, I courted a tenant's wife; she had already agreed. At the moment of consummation, she said she wanted to rely on me as a proper husband. I suddenly came to my senses and said "Must Not" four times, refusing to go through with it. That very night after I returned, you were conceived. This is Heaven rewarding me for not defiling another man's wife. If it were an ill omen, why golden characters? Why four "Must Not," matching what I once said? This is a good sign.' The son agreed. He immediately wrote to a fellow examinee; the next year he was reinstated. Later he rose to Vice Minister, and the whole family flourished.

This passage illustrates that sons of wealthy families must be careful not to sow their seed with another man. A retired official who had served as magistrate had four sons, all licentiates (xiucai), clever and handsome. One day the official died. A geomancer selected a burial site with excellent fengshui, saying: "Within six years and two examination cycles, all four young masters will pass." Six years later, the geomancer came to collect his reward. The three elder sons had all passed and become officials; only the fourth son remained at home entertaining the geomancer. He respectfully asked: "You promised all four of us would pass. My three brothers have indeed succeeded. In talent I am even superior to them; why do I alone fail?" The next day, the geomancer and the fourth son climbed the grave to examine it closely. The geomancer said: "By this site, all the brothers should pass; if one has not, there must be a reason." The son pressed him for an explanation. The geomancer asked: "How old was your late father when he begot you?" The son replied: "Father was sixty when I was born; he died at seventy-four; that makes another six years now." He asked again: "How old was your mother then?" The son said: "Thirty." The geomancer shook his head: "I know now." The son asked: "What do you know?" The geomancer said: "Do not take offense. If you wish to pass, you must ask the old lady whose blood you truly are." The son understood. That night he set up a lavish feast and slowly got his mother drunk. After the second watch, he instructed relatives and servants to retire first. With no one around, he knelt and said: "I have something I dare not speak. Does Mother wish me to pass?" The mother said: "Your three brothers all passed; I desire your success most of all. Whatever it is, good or bad, just say it." The son said: "The geomancer says I am not Father's own flesh and blood, which is why I don't pass. I must know who truly fathered me before I can succeed." The mother loved her youngest son; it was a quiet night, no one else was present, and she was drunk—she let slip: "The geomancer sees truly. At that time your father was already sixty. A certain page in the yamen was young and handsome; I actually bore you by him." The son obtained the truth. The next day he consulted the geomancer. The geomancer said: "You must go there, retrieve the page's bones, and bury them beside the grave; in the next cycle you will pass." The son followed these instructions, fetched and buried them; in the next cycle he indeed passed.

This passage reveals how illegitimate offspring can be concealed, unknown to others—hence why some share the same ancestral fortune yet end up worlds apart in rank. There is always something unspeakable about such matters.

Another case: the father of a certain Xie had failing vitality and no son. In the summer heat, his mother was sleeping on the bed in a thin unlined skirt when a male monkey kept by the household came and violated her. Startled awake, she tried to push it off, but the monkey bared its teeth and claws to bite and scratch, so she could not push it away. As she drifted back into a deep sleep, her spirits stirred, passion rose in her despite herself, and she conceived. When Xie's father returned home, his wife told him how the monkey had violated her and said, "This unnatural creature must be killed." Feeling guilty after the deed, the monkey had climbed up a tall peach tree outside the back gate and refused to come down. Xie's father deliberately sported with his wife beneath the tree; seeing them make love, the monkey grew excited and climbed down, whereupon Xie's father clubbed it to death and buried it under the peach tree. Later, when young Xie was born, he was extraordinarily bright and quick-witted, yet he hopped and tumbled on the ground just like a monkey. His mother knew in her heart that he was the monkey's seed, but having no other son, she could not bear to kill him. When the boy was eight, his father died. A geomancer chose a burial site and said, "This site is superb; it will produce a child prodigy and a man of great talent. Though the boy seems unruly now, in three years he will rise to high rank." Three years later, the geomancer returned. Mother Xie said, "You said that after three years this boy would mend his ways, yet he is still as wild and flighty as before—what can be done?" The geomancer went back to inspect the grave carefully, then returned and asked, "Madam, was this boy born of your own womb, or of a concubine?" Mother Xie replied, "He is not my own; a neighbor's maid bore him by a monkey and wanted to abandon him. Because I had no son, I took him in from birth and raised him as my own." The geomancer said, "If you want this boy to amount to something, the monkey's bones must be buried beside this grave; then in days to come he will bring great prosperity to your house." Mother Xie dug beneath the peach tree and found the bones still there. She went expressly to tell the geomancer, "The neighbors still have the bones; how should we handle it?" The geomancer instructed her to choose an auspicious day to bury them. After another three years, the boy was indeed recommended as a child prodigy and later became a celebrated figure of his age. (Heard from Geomancer Chen of that district.)

This passage shows that the effect of feng shui is as immediate as a shadow and an echo. Families who secure a good site must ensure their descendants observe rites and laws; they must not ruin their virtue through lust, lest they squander the family fortune for others.

stories.title_en: A Wicked Maid Steals the Silver

paragraphs.en: In Ningcheng lived a man named Li Ying, over twenty years old, clever and slick, yet addicted to wine and women. He often bought summer cloth, went outside Chang Gate in Suzhou, and lodged at broker Chen Si's shop, which also sold white liquor. A neighbor, Lin Tingjie, frequently sent his maid Jing Ji to buy wine. Ji was only eighteen, a rare beauty. Li Ying fell for her, teased her into an affair, and bought hairpins and bangles for her. Others in the shop often warned him not to court disaster. Ying and Ji were both young and deeply in love—who would sever such a bond? Later, Tingjie discovered their affair. He called Ji and scolded her: "You have been secretly with Guest Li; I will let you off this once. Secretly watch where Ying hides his silver, steal some, and I will get you clothes to enjoy later."

One day, while Ying was out drinking at a brothel, the courtesan Jing Ji quietly unlocked his room and stole over a hundred taels of silver. When Ying returned to the inn and discovered the silver missing, he pressed the innkeeper to make good the loss. Fellow lodger Wu Lun said, "When you keep silver in your room, you shouldn't go drinking far off at a brothel; even if you do, you should return early. You went out carousing and lost it—what does that have to do with the innkeeper? At noon today I saw Jing Ji go into your room; it must be that woman who stole it. You can report this to the officials, and the innkeeper and I will testify for you."

Ying waited two days; Ji did not come to the shop, so he reported it to the prefecture. Tingjie claimed Ying had seduced his maid. When the affair was exposed, fearing prosecution, Ji had first falsely accused Ying of losing silver to cover his tracks. Prefect Zhang questioned the witnesses. Wu Lun and Chen Si testified: "We saw Ji enter Ying's room with our own eyes; it is true he stole the silver." Prefect Zhang pressed: "A guest's room and a maiden's bed—neither should be entered lightly. If you saw Ji enter Ying's room, why didn't you stop him?" Lun said: "Ying and Ji having an affair is also true; so when Ying wasn't in the shop, Ji opened the door and stole." Prefect Zhang found this out and knew the silver was indeed stolen by Ji; but Tingjie was a student of the prefectural school, ranked second in the last exam, so he followed Tingjie's complaint and ruled: "Since there was an illicit affair, the lost silver is merely a covering excuse. Li Ying was wrong to seduce a serving maid and then lie. Chen Si, as broker, knew of the affair; why didn't he advise Ying to stop sooner? After it blew up, he still testified one-sidedly. Each is sentenced to beating."

Note: This judgment was very unjust to Li Ying. Especially as a traveling merchant, one should be careful and self-restrained; who has an affair with someone's maid and does not bring disaster? Nowadays many shops use wives and daughters to lure guests; after the affair they cheat them of their capital. See through this trick; do not fall into it.

stories.title_en: Seduction of a Broker's Daughter Ends in a Swindle

paragraphs.en: Broker Liao San, alias Longtan, had a daughter named Shuji, just sixteen, still unmarried. Her face shone like the moon goddess, her beauty rivaling a flower immortal—truly the leader among women, unmatched in the world. The merchant Zhang Lu, a little over twenty, handsome and elegant, well-versed in poetry and books, drifted from place to place. One day he bought several dozen loads of Fujian bamboo shoots and sold them at Liao San's shop. Due to frequent delays, the goods were sold on credit, with the silver still unpaid. Over time, seeing the daughter's charming looks, he longed day and night and could not sleep. But Liao San's household was crowded, making it hard to act. The girl also sometimes peeked at Lu from behind the door. Lu made eyes at her; she lowered her head in a shy pose. Their hearts were already joined, but the path remained blocked, like the Magpie Bridge hard to cross.

One day, Liao San's household rose early to prepare breakfast. He then went with some merchants to the countryside to collect debts. Zhang Lu, delighted by this opportunity, slipped into her room and committed adultery with Liao's daughter. Afterward, they continued to meet privately from time to time.

When the mother found out, she conferred with her husband: "How many wealthy families have sought our daughter's hand, and we refused to give her lightly! Now she has been defiled by this rat of a traveling merchant. We must secretly catch and kill him to vent our anger." Liao San said, "No. Only when a wife commits adultery and you catch them in the act and kill both on the spot does the law hold you blameless. Here it is our daughter having an illicit affair: I cannot bear to kill them both, and if we kill only the merchant, his offense does not carry the death penalty—how could we kill him without facing serious consequences afterward? Right now the bamboo-shoot accounts are settled, and all his silver is in my hands. Let us secretly watch for when our daughter meets him again, catch them in the act, beat him half to death, chain him up, and force a written confession out of him. Won't he have to forfeit his bamboo-shoot silver to us then? And what would he dare say afterward?" His wife agreed.

Within days Zhang Lu fell into the trap. Lu said: "This is my own fault. Give me back half the silver and let it go; otherwise I cannot rest." Liao San refused, so Lu sued at the prefecture, where the case was remanded to the court. Judge Wu uncovered the truth and asked Shuji: "Have you been betrothed?" She replied: "Not yet." He then asked Lu: "Are you married?" Lu already had a wife but lied: "My first wife is dead; I have not remarried." Judge Wu ruled: "Since neither of you is married, you must be joined; the silver extorted shall count as the bride-price." Liao San argued: "If a man who seduces a virgin can then marry her, how will others be warned?" Judge Wu retorted: "You matchmakers often use wives and daughters to trap guests into affairs and cheat them out of their silver—do I not know? If they are not matched, I will have your daughter sold by the government and investigate the silver; Zhang Lu will still be punished for adultery." Lu protested: "How is one girl worth over a hundred taels of bride-price? Order half returned to me, counting as her dowry." Judge Wu declared: "A merchant visiting brothels should still observe limits; how dare he seduce the host's virgin daughter?" Lu felt both gratitude and shame, weeping; he lost all his capital, gained only a wife, and had no travel funds left, so he sold her hand for thirty taels and returned home.

Note: Brokers who connive with their wives and daughters to commit adultery with guests, then cheat them out of their capital—this is a common trick. Pity this girl did not know she was being sold by her parents; Zhang Lu also did not know and fell into the trap. Luckily Judge Wu ordered them married; though he lost his money, he still got a wife. Pity his capital was so thin he could not take the girl home. For merchants in the future: relying on such legal resolutions is fundamentally unrealistic; one must be very careful to guard against being cheated through an affair.
